summary: Weekly POC sync covering last sprint's prefetch experiments, KV/prefix cache hit rate deltas, and prompt-reuse tradeoffs. We reviewed two eviction policies, a session-affinity tweak, and early latency/cost numbers. Agreed next steps: 24h stress run, share eviction scripts, and pricing update.
transcript:
[00:00] Meeting header: 2026-03-29 15:00 UTC | Duration 42m | Attendees: Samira (Redwood), Julian (Redwood), Devon (Redwood), Maya (Kestrel), Ravi (Kestrel), Laura (Kestrel), Tom (Kestrel)

[00:12] Samira (Redwood): All right everyone thanks for joining. quick agenda: we want to run through the sprint results for the prefetch experiments, look at hit rates and the eviction comparison, and decide the next run. anything to add?

[00:25] Maya (Kestrel): Nope that covers it. we've got the logs from last night, and ravi has some aggregated numbers.

[00:33] Ravi (Kestrel): yeah i'll start. so we ran A/B between policy A which is LRU-based with 20min TTL on inferred prefixes, and policy B which is hybrid—session affinity plus priority buckets for recurring users. the headline: KV cache overall hit rose from 18% to 33% with policy B, prefix reuse improved about 9 points. but there is a small tail-latency increase under load.

[01:05] Julian (Redwood): can you clarify the tail? 99th percentile delta?

[01:09] Ravi (Kestrel): 99p went from 420ms to 580ms during the 2pm-3pm spike in our traffic generator. average token latency stayed similar. there's a bit more variability when the prefetching backend overlaps with long-running KV loads.

[01:35] Laura (Kestrel): we suspect some eviction storms when a cohort rotates - saw a lot of simultaneous invalidations which spiked disk I/O on the edge nodes.

[01:42] Devon (Redwood): that matches our lab runs; eviction storms happen when you warm too many large prefixes simultaneously. one mitigation is spreading prefetch windows and prioritizing smaller prefixes first. also batch the background prefetches with backpressure.

[02:04] Tom (Kestrel): does the hybrid session affinity require sticky routing? we're trying to avoid long-lived session pins in our VPC.

[02:12] Julian (Redwood): no, it's logical affinity not network sticky. we tag sessions and route to a pool with warmed KV snapshots; if the pool is overloaded we fallback to stateless. the routing is policy-driven in the runtime.

[02:36] Speaker 1: (inaudible) thread about cache sizing?

[02:40] Samira (Redwood): sizing is key — with B we used slightly larger reserved KV region which improved hit rates but of course increased cost. we'll show cost per 1M requests later.

[03:05] Maya (Kestrel): about the prompt reuse strategy — we tested small prompt coalescing where we canonicalize some system prompts and dedupe them before caching. that raised prefix reuse but introduced a two-step normalization latency for some paths. overall it shaved down token generation cost by ~6% though.

[03:33] Julian (Redwood): interesting. canonicalization complexity matters — simple deterministic trimming is cheap, but heavy semantic normalization can backfire. what did you normalize?

[03:45] Ravi (Kestrel): whitespace, sentence casing, plus canonical role markers. not embeddings or semantic hashes yet.

[03:56] Julian (Redwood): good choices. avoid semantic hashing until you have a stable prompt distribution.

[04:12] Laura (Kestrel): we also rolled a small experiment with prefix coalescing where similar prefixes share a cached KV snapshot. that helped for conversational handoffs but complicated eviction logic.

[04:28] Devon (Redwood): right, coalescing increases reuse but risks larger cold misses when you evict, since coalesced entries are heavier. that's the tradeoff.

[04:45] Tom (Kestrel): security question — when you coalesce across users, any risk of data bleed? we need to be conscious of PHI handling.

[04:54] Julian (Redwood): we never coalesce across tenant boundaries. all coalescing is within the same tenant and with tenant-scoped keys. for PHI we recommend token-level filtering before caching and stricter TTLs.

[05:12] Maya (Kestrel): ok good. audit logs — can you keep an action-level audit when eviction or prefetch touches a key? we need that for compliance.

[05:21] Devon (Redwood): yes runtime emits audit events for cache mutations; we can extend retention for the pilot. we'll attach doc.

[05:32] Samira (Redwood): quick pause — can we show the chart Ravi mentioned?

[05:36] Ravi (Kestrel): sharing screen... (brief pause) here's the daily heatmap. you can see an increase in clustered hits for returning sessions after the hybrid policy. blue is hit-rate, red is disk activity.

[06:05] Julian (Redwood): looks like the hotspot coincides with your background prefetch window at minute 5 of each session. can we jitter that window to smooth load?

[06:15] Ravi (Kestrel): we didn't jitter in this run, good call. we'll add jitter and run again.

[06:22] Laura (Kestrel): another observation: the model V we used for the A run has a bigger KV footprint; switching to the V-quantized variant reduced memory pressure but slightly reduced quality in edge cases.

[06:37] Devon (Redwood): quantized models change the memory tradeoffs but shouldn't change prefix semantics. if quality drop is small, the cost wins might be worth it. we should quantify regression with a few prompt tests.

[06:56] Tom (Kestrel): customers will ask about fallback strategy — when warmed pool is saturated do we fallback to smaller model or to hosted Redwood endpoints?

[07:06] Julian (Redwood): policy can fallback to a lower-cost model variant in the same pool, route to hosted instance, or queue briefly. your choice in config. we recommend model variant fallback first to preserve latency.

[07:22] Maya (Kestrel): what's the observed cost delta when using the hybrid policy and coalescing?

[07:29] Ravi (Kestrel): early estimates: unit cost down ~12% due to token reuse and fewer redundant decodes, despite a 6% bump in infra spend for reserved KV capacity. net savings about 6% in our pilot numbers.

[07:45] Samira (Redwood): ok that's within expected range. we'll produce a more detailed cost model per 1M requests.

[07:54] Speaker 2: (background) are we comfortable with the 20min TTL?

[08:00] Julian (Redwood): 20min is a starting point. in many workloads shorter TTLs with higher prefetch frequency and smaller buckets do better. longer TTLs help when sessions are very bursty. it's workload-dependent.

[08:17] Ravi (Kestrel): we ran sensitivity: TTL 5/20/60 minutes. 5min lowered cost but reduced reuse dramatically. 60min increased reuse but memory costs balloon. 20 felt like a middle.

[08:33] Maya (Kestrel): for compliance we might prefer shorter TTLs for certain endpoints. can we have per-route TTL config?

[08:40] Julian (Redwood): yes per-route TTL is supported in the config layer.

[08:47] Laura (Kestrel): one more: we saw GC-like pauses in our edge node logs during big evictions. might be the language runtime or the storage engine doing compaction. any recs?

[08:58] Devon (Redwood): try bounded eviction batches and staggered compaction; also tune storage flush thresholds to avoid synchronous compactions during spikes. we'll share the tuning parameters.

[09:18] Samira (Redwood): let's discuss the proposed 24h stress run. objective: validate eviction policy B at scale, with jittered prefetch windows, and quantized model variant fallback enabled. who owns?

[09:30] Maya (Kestrel): we'll run it on our staging cluster. expecting to start 2026-04-01 and run 24h.

[09:37] Ravi (Kestrel): we'll collect 1m request sample every hour and share traces.

[09:44] Samira (Redwood): great. Julian will provide scripts and the eviction policy parameters. Samira will update pricing. Devon will extend audit retention.

[10:00] Tom (Kestrel): procurement/legal question — if we move to private deployment, what's the typical audit log retention options and KMS integrations?

[10:10] Devon (Redwood): we support customer KMS/HSM integrations and can enable longer audit retention as an add-on. we'll send the compliance pack after the call.

[10:22] Maya (Kestrel): competitor note: some teams here mentioned Anthropic's managed offering for simplified caching, and Vertex for integrated GCP routing. curious how Redwood compares on operational visibility.

[10:35] Julian (Redwood): our differentiator is fine-grain observability per-model/per-route and the rollout controls—canary, percentage rollouts, automatic fallback. we'll send a short doc comparing observability features.

[10:50] Samira (Redwood): any blockers to the plan?

[10:54] Laura (Kestrel): none from SRE; just need the eviction scripts and jitter patch.

[10:58] Ravi (Kestrel): once we run the 24h test we'll evaluate tail-latency and cost tradeoffs and decide on the pilot expansion.

[11:12] Samira (Redwood): recap: Kestrel runs 24h stress with policy B + jitter + quantized fallback; Julian uploads eviction scripts; Samira sends pricing; Devon sends audit retention options and compliance pack. we'll reconvene after test results.

[11:30] Tom (Kestrel): can we schedule the follow-up for the week of April 6th?

[11:35] Samira (Redwood): yes i'll propose times in the invite. thanks everyone.

[11:40] (end)

Notes on transcription: occasional overlap and some garbled words in the heatmap section. technical terms sometimes spelled phonetically (e.g., "K-V cash" for KV cache).
